analysis.one_liner: Makes oil spillers pay for cleanup and compensates victims through an industry-financed trust fund.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to three House committees, the bill never received a hearing or a vote; on August 3, 1989 the record pointed its substance to H.R. 1465, the vehicle for what became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the months after the Exxon Valdez spill, this bill would have made the company responsible for an oil spill strictly liable for cleanup and damages, created an industry-fee-financed Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund to cover claims beyond the spiller's liability cap, and required tankers and offshore facilities to prove they could pay before entering U.S. waters. It also would have let fishermen, coastal property owners, states, and Indian tribes collect for lost profits, property, and subsistence use. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishermen, subsistence users, and property owners near spills could recover lost profits, property damage, and lost subsistence use directly from the responsible party [S3]. State, local, and tribal governments could recover natural resource restoration costs as trustees and draw emergency cleanup money immediately, including up to $50,000 without prior approval [S3]. Taxpayers gain protection because the responsible party, not the Treasury, is the primary payer, with a fund financed by fees on oil as the backstop [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishermen, tribes, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Makes the party responsible for a spill strictly, jointly, and severally liable for removal and restoration costs, so the polluter rather than the taxpayer pays first

Lets people who live off affected waters recover for lost profits or earning capacity (if they derive at least 25% of earnings from the resource), damaged property, lost property taxes and royalties, and lost subsistence use
Funds an Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund financed by fees on oil to pay claims beyond the spiller's liability, and lets governors and tribal officials draw money immediately for emergency response

Requires vessels over 300 gross tons and offshore facilities to prove financial responsibility (insurance, bond, or guarantee) before using U.S. ports and waters, with clearance withheld or entry denied for noncompliance
Recognizes states and Indian tribes as trustees for damaged natural resources, and allows a civil penalty of up to $10 million when a resource cannot be restored or replaced

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, tanker and vessel owners, and offshore facility operators, through strict liability for spill costs, mandatory proof of financial responsibility, and fees on oil financing the trust fund; marine insurers and guarantors face direct claims. Some of these costs would pass through to consumers in the price of oil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies, tanker owners, and insurers

drawbacks.text: Liability is capped: $500 per gross ton (maximum $78 million) for tankers, $300 per gross ton or $500,000 for other vessels, and $75 million for facilities, so costs from a catastrophic spill beyond the cap shift to the trust fund rather than the spiller
The trust fund itself is capped at $500 million per incident unless the President waives the limit, which could leave major victims unpaid after the worst disasters
Claimants must first present claims to the responsible party and can wait up to 180 days before turning to the fund or court, delaying payment to people with damaged livelihoods
A party found less than 30% liable is only severally, not jointly, liable, which can leave victims short if other defendants cannot pay their shares
All oil-spill suits are confined to federal district courts, barring victims from state courts where they might otherwise file

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is a strong polluter-pays system: the party that creates the spill risk bears the cleanup and compensation costs, and the fee-financed fund backstops victims rather than taxpayers. The real concessions to industry are the liability caps ($78 million for tankers, $75 million for facilities) and the $500 million fund cap — significant, because a disaster on the scale of the Exxon Valdez, whose cleanup ran to billions, would exceed them. Still, the bill would have shifted a risk that historically fell on fishing families, coastal towns, and the Treasury onto the companies that profit from moving oil.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees without a hearing or vote, and in August 1989 the House pointed anyone following it to H.R. 1465 — a companion oil-spill bill that went on to become the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 — so this version simply expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert W. Davis, a Michigan Republican, introduced the bill on May 11, 1989 with the '(by request)' notation, the designation used when a bill is filed at the administration's request rather than on the sponsor's own initiative

The same day, the bill was referred jointly to three committees — Public Works and Transportation, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Ways and Means — a joint referral that let any one of them hold it

In late May 1989 the Water Resources and Coast Guard and Navigation subcommittees took referrals and the House requested comments from seven federal agencies (Commerce, Justice, State, DOE, DOT, EPA, and CEQ); the record shows no hearing or markup afterward
Not a single cosponsor signed on during the bill's three months on the calendar
On August 3, 1989 the action record closes with 'See H.R. 1465,' routing the bill's substance to another oil-spill measure — the bill that became the Oil Pollution Act of 1990
The Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with this bill never having come to a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public lost little, because Congress enacted essentially the same liability-and-fund system through H.R. 1465 (the Oil Pollution Act of 1990). The main beneficiaries of this particular bill's death were oil and shipping interests, which gained several more months before stricter liability rules took effect.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no partisan split appears in the record: a Republican carried the administration's bill while the Democratic-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill makes oil companies strictly liable for spills from their vessels, pipelines, and offshore facilities, imposes per-barrel fees to finance the trust fund, and requires proof of financial responsibility. Its interest in capping and avoiding spill costs runs against the public's interest in being made whole.

Tanker liability would run up to $500 per gross ton (capped at $78 million), and vessels without certified financial responsibility could be denied entry to U.S. ports. The bill directly targets the tanker practices that produced the spills prompting it.

Guarantors face direct claims from spill victims and must underwrite mandatory financial-residency certificates, expanding their exposure. Insurers historically backed liability caps, which this bill preserves but tightens around.

These businesses gain a clear federal right to recover lost profits and earning capacity from the spiller — the people the Exxon Valdez left with unpaid losses. Their interest and the public's point the same way.

Governments become natural-resource trustees who recover restoration costs and can draw emergency cleanup funds immediately, rather than waiting on the polluter or Congress. This shifts response power and money closer to affected communities.
